findings.claim: Odimba "sets Princess & The Hustler in 1963 Bristol"; lesson 2 repeats "The play is set during the Bristol Bus Boycott of 1963" and "Setting: St Pauls, Bristol, 1963"; the lesson 1 knowledge check asks "In what year is Princess & The Hustler set?" and marks 1963 as the only right answer.
findings.truth: Act 1 Scene 1 is Christmas Day 1962, months before the boycott began on 30 April 1963. Act 2 is May 1963, Act 3 August 1963, and the final scene a month later. The play runs from Christmas 1962 into late 1963.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 1 Scene 1: 'Christmas Day, 1962, in the James family home in Bristol' (litcharts.com/lit/princess-the-hustler/act-1-scene-1); Live Theatre synopsis 'The play begins on Christmas Day 1962'; GradeSaver act dates (May / August / September).

findings.claim: Timeline entry dated 28 August 1963: "Raghbir Singh becomes the first non-white bus conductor."
findings.truth: Ian Patey announced the end of the colour bar on 28 August 1963. Raghbir Singh started as Bristol's first non-white bus conductor on 17 September 1963.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Bristol Bus Boycott; BlackPast.org, 'The Bristol Bus Boycott of 1963'.

findings.claim: Taught across five lessons: "Princess narrates much of the play"; "She addresses the audience directly, breaking the fourth wall"; "Princess is the play's protagonist and narrator"; "short scenes linked by Princess's narration"; "Epic theatre: Direct address ... echo Brechtian techniques". Lesson 2 knowledge check 2 marks "Breaking the fourth wall" correct; lesson 6 practice question 5 asks students to analyse "Princess's narrative voice" and "the effect of direct address".
findings.truth: There is no narrator and no direct address. The play opens with Princess alone, eyes closed, in the cupboard room in a swimming costume and sash; a VOICE-OVER announces her as winner of the Weston-super-Mare Beauties of the West Contest, and the cupboard room explodes into staged pageantry. Her inner world reaches the audience through staged fantasy sequences, not narration. In a closed-book exam this would send students to write about a dramatic method the play does not use.
findings.evidence: Published opening stage direction of Scene One (quoted in search results from the Nick Hern script); LitCharts Princess character page: content does not indicate she narrates or addresses the audience; LitCharts Act 3 Scene 6: 'The text does not indicate that Princess addresses the audience directly'; Susan Elkin review of the Bristol Old Vic premiere: no narration, conventional fourth-wall staging.

findings.claim: "Mavis reveals in Act 2 that after Jamaican military service, Wendell was promised a decent job in England but given a much lower position"; repeated in lesson 5 and in a lesson 2 knowledge check and flashcard.
findings.truth: Wendell served in the ENGLISH army and was discharged in the 1940s with a lung condition. The good job he was promised on his return never materialised. The point of the backstory is that he served Britain and Britain broke its promise; 'Jamaican military service' loses that and is simply wrong.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Wendell character page: 'He served in the English army but was discharged with a lung condition in the 1940s. Upon return, he was promised a good job that never materialized.'

findings.claim: "Crucially, Odimba also includes white allies. Students from the University of Bristol, church groups, and progressive trade unionists join the boycott ... This is historically accurate." Repeated in lesson 7 ("White students, church members, and progressive workers support the boycott"), in a lesson 3 knowledge check, a lesson 3 flashcard ("historically accurate"), and two practice-question mark schemes.
findings.truth: The play has seven characters: Princess, Mavis, Wendell, Wendell Junior, Lorna, Margot and Leon. No students, church members or trade unionists appear. The only white character is Margot, Mavis's 42-year-old neighbour, who dismisses the campaign and accuses Wendell of using it for his own ends. Historically the claim is also wrong in one part: the local TGWU upheld the colour bar and only voted to end it on 27 August 1963 (lesson 1 correctly says the TGWU enforced it). Bristol University students did march on 1 May 1963, and Bristol East MP Tony Benn backed the boycott.
findings.evidence: LitCharts and Shalom Education character lists (seven characters); LitCharts summary on Margot; Wikipedia and TUC 150 Stories on the TGWU's role and the 1 May student march.

findings.claim: Margot "evolution from sceptic to ally is genuine" (lesson 5); "from resistance to grudging respect" (lesson 3); "the white neighbour who evolved from sceptic to ally in Act 2" (lesson 4).
findings.truth: Margot never comes round to the boycott. She criticises Wendell for using civil-rights activism opportunistically and questions Mavis's renewed trust in him. She falls out with Mavis, then shelters Princess when she runs away and is welcomed back. The solidarity is personal, not political, and it happens in Act 3, not Act 2.
findings.evidence: LitCharts summary and Margot description; Shalom Education character analysis ('Margot displays casual racism, dismissing immigrant concerns about employment discrimination during Bus Boycott discussions').

findings.claim: A whole section, "Princess's Final Narration": "Her final narration brings together the threads of the story"; "Princess's final speech functions as an epilogue. She speaks to the audience about the future"; "The play ends as it began — with Princess addressing the audience." Carried into two knowledge checks, three flashcards, a practice question and its mark scheme, and lesson 6's cyclical-framing material.
findings.truth: Act 3 Scene 6 is set a month after the boycott succeeds. Princess directs Wendell to dress as a woman and act as the pageant compère; he announces her the winner and crowns her; a parade of finely dressed Black women fills the stage and Princess joins them to take a bow. There is no closing speech and no address to the audience. The structure is still cyclical, but through the pageant fantasy that also opens the play.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 3 Scene 6 summary; LitCharts full summary ('Princess has Wendell dress as a woman ... a line of beautiful Black female dancers'); Susan Elkin's review notes the closing recitation of the names of Black women.

findings.claim: "Relationship with Wendell: Their marriage is tested but not broken. She challenges him, worries about him, and ultimately respects him — a partnership of equals under pressure."
findings.truth: Wendell walked out about ten years before the play, fathered Lorna with another woman in Liverpool, and Mavis raised two children alone. She threatens him with a knife when he returns and forgives him only after he proves himself; he proposes marriage again at the end. 'A partnership of equals under pressure' misdescribes the whole relationship.
findings.evidence: Shalom Education character analysis (Mavis 'harbors deep anger toward Wendall for abandoning the family'; Act 1 'Mavis threatens him with a knife'); LitCharts Wendell page (Lorna's mother in Liverpool).

findings.claim: "Odimba populates the play with supporting characters who represent the wider St Pauls community. Neighbours, friends, and fellow boycotters appear throughout"; "When the family is in crisis, the community rallies"; "The supporting cast echoes the real individuals — Paul Stephenson, Roy Hackett, and others." Lesson 6 adds "Ensemble moments: Community scenes punctuate the family drama" and "Multi-roling: Actors may play multiple community roles". Lesson 7 adds "Neighbours function as an extended family network". A practice question and a flashcard test the same fabrication.
findings.truth: The cast is seven. Outside the James family there are exactly two characters: Margot (white neighbour, 42) and Leon (Junior's friend, 19). No boycott organiser appears on stage, no ensemble or community scene exists, and with seven named parts there is no multi-roling. The boycott reaches the family as news carried into the flat.
findings.evidence: LitCharts character list; Shalom Education 'Complete character list'; Susan Elkin's review names six principals plus Leon.

findings.claim: "Act 2 moves between private and public spaces — the street, the bus stop, community meetings"; lesson 3 knowledge check 1 marks "The play shifts from domestic space to public space" as the main Act 1 to Act 2 structural shift; lesson 6 refers to "the wider streets of St Pauls".
findings.truth: Study guides describe the play as taking place mostly in the James family's flat, with occasional scenes at the Bristol docks; Act 1 already goes to the docks. I could not confirm any street, bus-stop or community-meeting scene. Two defensible corrections: (a) replace the named locations with 'the docks' and keep the domestic-to-public point, or (b) drop the structural-shift claim and the knowledge check with it. Needs a look at the script to choose.
findings.evidence: Shalom Education: 'mostly takes place in the James family's flat, although the occasional scene takes place on the Bristol Docks'; LitCharts Act 1 (Wendell takes the girls to the docks).

findings.claim: Lesson 7: "Cultural expression, self-naming (Princess), and asserting presence are acts of resistance." Lesson 5: the name is "her parents' aspiration for her".
findings.truth: Her given name is Phyllis James; 'Princess' is what she is called. The two lessons contradict each other on who named her, and I could not establish it from any source. Recommend cutting 'self-naming' from lesson 7 unless the script supports it.

findings.claim: All seven lessons place the family in St Pauls ("Setting: St Pauls, Bristol"; "the wider community of St Pauls"; "the wider streets of St Pauls").
findings.truth: Every source I checked places the play in Bristol without naming the neighbourhood; LitCharts explicitly says the neighbourhood is not identified. St Pauls is where Bristol's West Indian community lived and is a reasonable inference, but it is taught here as a fact. Recommend confirming from the script; if Odimba does not name it, soften to 'Bristol'. I have left it in place rather than change something I cannot verify.
findings.evidence: LitCharts full summary: 'The specific neighborhood within Bristol is not identified'; AQA, Bristol Old Vic and Nick Hern blurbs say only '1960s Bristol'.

findings.claim:
Malformed markup:

The Crisis: Princess Goes Missing

... Princess's Final Narration. The n13 heading is never closed, so the second heading text renders as loose body text.
findings.truth: A nested-heading defect from an earlier patch, not a factual error. My edit corrects the heading wording but does not repair the nesting. Worth fixing when the edits are applied.

findings.claim: "Caribbean music (ska, calypso, gospel)" and "protest songs connect the Bristol boycott to the wider civil rights movement"; lesson 3 adds "Caribbean music, church hymns, and protest songs".
findings.truth: I could not verify the specific genres or the protest songs against the script or any review. Low risk to marks, but it is invented-sounding detail. Flagged only.
findings.evidence: No source found naming the music cues.

findings.claim: The lesson 2 key-fact revision tip still reads "what makes Princess's child narration distinctive".
findings.truth: After the F3 fixes the word 'narration' in that revision-tip attribute is stale. I left the attribute byte-identical rather than edit it, because the brief tells me to keep those attributes intact. The tip still works ('what three qualities does her voice combine?'). Re-word it if attribute edits are acceptable.

exam_claims_verified: All 42 practice questions are labelled '30+4 marks — Modern Text Essay' with the split Critical response 12 / Methods 12 / Context 6 / SPaG 4, which matches AQA Paper 2 Section A (AO1 12, AO2 12, AO3 6, plus 4 SPaG; one essay from a choice of two; no printed extract; closed book; 2h15 paper). No 'Shakespeare' or '19th-century' mislabels, no 'AO2 is not assessed' claim, and no banned strings anywhere in the unit.
summary: Seven lessons, 15 findings (5 HIGH, 5 MEDIUM, 5 LOW), 79 edits across all seven lessons; no lesson is clean. The history and the exam framing are sound, but the unit invents three things about the play itself and teaches them in knowledge checks, flashcards and practice questions: that Princess narrates and breaks the fourth wall (she does not — the play is conventional fourth-wall staging with sung-in fantasy sequences), that the play ends with her epilogue to the audience (it ends with Wendell in a dress crowning her at a fantasy pageant), and that an ensemble of white student, church and trade-union allies joins the boycott (the cast is seven, and the one white character opposes the campaign). Wendell's army service is also wrongly called Jamaican when he served in the English army — which reverses the point of his betrayal.
